title: Savitri at the banyan
hook: a banyan wound with thread: how Savitri's story became a vrata, a vow kept with the body
carry: a vrata turns a story into a vow

segments.voice: Yesterday, satsang: on the road behind Death, Savitri showed that time near the good is never wasted.
screen: `TIME NEAR THE GOOD IS NEVER WASTED.`

segments.voice: A banyan tree, its trunk wound round and round with thread. On a festival day called Vat Savitri, some married Hindu women fast, walk around a banyan and tie thread to it, asking for long lives for their husbands. The tree doesn't come from the epic's telling; it comes from the way the story has been lived since. On our last day with her: how a story becomes a vow, and how one woman can be read more than one way.
screen: `A BANYAN WOUND WITH THREAD.` → `A FESTIVAL IN HER NAME.` → `ONE WOMAN, MORE THAN ONE READING.`

segments.voice: Start with where the epic puts her. The story sits in the Mahabharata's forest book, in a section whose title can be translated as the greatness of the devoted wife. The sage Markandeya tells it because Yudhishthira has asked: has there ever been a woman as devoted as Draupadi? His answer is Savitri, and his last word is that Draupadi, like Savitri, will save them all. So the frame is devotion, and some readers keep it: a wife whose faithfulness is strong enough to stop Death. Others hear a woman of fierce will and a sharp mind, who chose her own husband, kept a hard truth alone for a year, and argued with Death on the road. A modern poet, Aurobindo, read her as the divine word come down to free the soul from death. Now the teaching. Hinduism has a name for what happens at the banyan: a vrata, a vow. You choose a day, you fast or keep a rule, you do a puja, and you hear the story the vow belongs to, its vrat katha, told out loud. Hindus keep vratas for Shiva, for the Goddess, on Ekadashi, for the people they love. On Vat Savitri, the story is Savitri's. And Savitri kept one herself: before the day Death came, the epic says, she held a three-night vow, fasting and standing still like a post. The women at the tree are doing a smaller version of what she did. That's the gift of a vrata in a busy life. Love that would stay a feeling becomes a day you keep, with an empty stomach and a thread in your hand.
screen: `THE GREATNESS OF THE DEVOTED WIFE` · `DEVOTION, WILL, THE DIVINE WORD` · `VRATA: A FAST, A PUJA, A STORY TOLD` · `SAVITRI KEPT ONE HERSELF` · then, large: `A VRATA TURNS A STORY INTO A VOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose life you'd ask to be long, and hold their face for a moment. Then, slowly, as if winding thread around a banyan, go round them in your mind, their morning, their work, their evening, their sleep, one slow circle for each breath. If you pray, you can pray for them, the way the women at the tree do.
Savitri. Told as the greatness of a devoted wife, read by others as a woman of will, and kept each year in a vrata at a banyan wound with thread.
Your line: a vrata turns a story into a vow. Savitri's became a thread around a banyan. Rest well.
